The multilevel literature adds a caution about the standard error of such a term. @HeisigSchaeffer2019WhyYouShould [p. 258] argue that "multilevel models involving cross-level interactions should always include random slopes on the lower-level components of those interactions", because without them the test of the interaction is "severely anti-conservative", and the warning of Stegmueller about cross-level interactions with few countries, quoted in section 3, applies to the same term. The published model tests its interactions with random intercepts only. A footnote of the paper reports that "[r]andom slopes models show similar regression coefficients to the random intercept model" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 631, n. 3], but similar coefficients say nothing about the standard errors on which the verdict depends, so a random slope for education across countries is one of the decisions that a reanalysis of this claim has to make.

**A replication exercise of your own.** The pieces for a second exercise in the style of the first are all on this page: a claim card, an estimand statement, a public dataset on which the aggregate design runs in the browser lab or the workspace, the respondent file for anyone who built it, and the published values of OA to reproduce. The menu is smaller than the one for the first claim, and each of its decisions is one that you can defend or not: the frame set, the scoring rule, the rule for the respondents who named nothing, the coding of education (the published three bands, or four bands that keep students separate), the estimator (random intercepts, fixed effects, or cells), the random part (random intercepts alone, or a random slope for education across countries), the sample, the weight, and whether growth enters beside unemployment. Fix one specification in a preregistration, as in Task 5, then run it and set the interaction that you get against the rows of the table above. The table already shows that two of those decisions, the design and the rule for the respondents who named nothing, decide whether the claim is found.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Refit `m_edu` above with `edu3 * munemp` replaced by `edu3 * mgrowth` alone, and read the growth interactions against the claim in the paper that "GDP growth impacts mainly on the EU framing of low-educated citizens" (p. 619). In the workspace the 810 cells are `data/EUframes_cy_edu.csv`, and section 6 of `prep/02_scales_and_panel.R` rebuilds the same cells from your respondent file as `by_edu`. Either file needs `unemp` and `growth` centred on their means over the 810 rows, as this page centres them, before the fit.

Then put the interaction to the respondents themselves. Adding `edu3:munemp + edu3:mgrowth` to `m_cosmo` of section 5 turns it into the published model with its interactions under the zero rule, and its coefficient on `edu3high:munemp` should match the row of the published model with the no-opinion respondents scored zero in @tbl-claim2. Fit the model once more with `s_util` as the outcome, and read the interaction that the paper found absent.
:::

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The specification is the published Table 3, Model 1, of OA with its cross-level interactions dropped, taken from the Stata code that the author provided to the SCORE dossier [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic]. Every model of the respondents was fitted once, locally, on the respondent file that the workspace builds from the sixteen GESIS waves, which is never committed and never redistributed; [the data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) explains that regime. The saved outputs of sections 3 and 9 come from `fit_models.R`, the numbers of the three random structures of section 3 from `fit_person_multilevel.R`, the published model of section 5 and the prevalence gradient of section 6 from `fit_person_anchor.R`, the fits with terms for the years of section 7 from `fit_person_years.R`, the fits of the second claim in section 10 from `fit_claim2.R`, and the refits of the published design from `R/eu-frames/13_reference_marks.R`, all in the folder `companion/_model-outputs/` but the last. The models in the live code of the page are fitted when the page is built, on the panel and the panel by education band, both of which ship with the site.

The vocabularies of section 1 come from the standard texts of each tradition: @RaudenbushBryk2002HierarchicalLinearModels and @SnijdersBosker2012MultilevelAnalysisIntroduction for sociology and education, @BeckKatz1995WhatNotTimeseries, @Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling and @Schmidt-CatranFairbrother2016RandomEffectsMultilevel for comparative data in political science and sociology, @Wooldridge2010EconometricAnalysisCross for econometrics, and @PinheiroBates2000MixedEffectsModelsSPLUS, @DeBruineBarr2021UnderstandingMixedeffectsModels, @HamakerMuthen2020FixedRandomEffects and @McNeishKelley2019FixedEffectsModels for psychology and biostatistics, with @GelmanHill2007DataAnalysisUsing on the conflicting definitions of fixed and random effects. The models are fitted with lme4 and lmerTest [@BatesEtAl2015FittingLinearMixedeffects; @KuznetsovaEtAl2017LmerTestPackageTests], fixest [@BergeEtAl2026FastUserfriendlyEconometrics], glmmTMB [@BrooksEtAl2017GlmmTMBBalancesSpeed] and ordbetareg [@Kubinec2023OrderedBetaRegression]. The within–between model is argued for by @BellJones2015ExplainingFixedEffects and @BellEtAl2019FixedRandomEffects, and the cautions about few countries and cross-level interactions are those of @BryanJenkins2016MultilevelModellingCountry, @Stegmueller2013HowManyCountries and @HeisigSchaeffer2019WhyYouShould.
